title: Let the Work Do the Talking
essay_markdown:
"How the hell can I ask the people who work for me to travel cheaply," Ingvar Kamprad reportedly said, before asking whether he should be traveling in luxury himself.

## The billionaire in economy class

Kamprad founded IKEA. He was born on a Swedish farm to a poor family, and he went on to build one of the best-known companies in the world. Yet he lived frugally, in a modest house, and flew economy class. He had every reason to announce his success, and he simply didn't. His life made the point for him.

Barry Sanders offers a second picture. The football star is remembered as someone who never showboated and never talked trash. He ran circles around defenders, and he retired early rather than chase the all-time rushing record, walking away as if it were no big deal. (Details vary by account, so treat the story as a sketch rather than a full biography.)

## Why quiet beats loud

Here is the idea at its simplest: you don't need to keep telling people how good you are. Constant self-promotion often grows out of a quiet doubt, a need to be reassured that you matter. Humility is what it looks like when you no longer need that reassurance. When your work is good, it speaks for itself, and it speaks more convincingly than you could.

One exception: on a resume or in an interview, showcasing your accomplishments is the job. Do it plainly and with confidence. The point isn't to hide what you've done. It's to stop *performing* it.

## Where this shows up

You've seen it at the dinner table, when someone steers every story back to their own win. You've seen it in the meeting where one person lists their contributions before anyone has asked. You've also met the opposite: the colleague who fixes things quietly, and whose reputation grows because people keep noticing.

## Try it today

- **Notice the urge.** When you feel the pull to mention an achievement, pause and ask who it's for. If it helps the other person, share it. If it only feeds your ego, let it go.
- **Ask a question instead.** Swap your story for curiosity about someone else's. People remember who listened.
- **Credit others out loud.** Name the teammate who helped. It costs you nothing and builds trust.
- **Do the work well and move on.** Finish something today without announcing it.

Kamprad didn't need the front of the plane to prove anything. You don't need the spotlight either.

Be so good that you never have to say it.

item.title: Be Humble
item.body: Arrogant people suffer from an inferiority complex, which is why they feel the need to parade their accomplishments. Learn to be humble. There’s no need to repeatedly talk about what you’ve achieved just to assert your ability — when your work is good, the results will speak for themselves. (The exception is in professional contexts like on your resume or in interviews, where you are supposed to showcase your accomplishments.)
